passages.title: The New Dog
sentences: A new dog came to the park.
He stood by the gate all alone.
His tail was down.
Pixel saw him.
Pixel ran over with his red ball.
He dropped it at the new dog's feet.
The new dog wagged his tail.
Then the two dogs ran and played until dark.
Sam smiled. "Pixel made a friend," he said.

passages.title: The Dog, the Cock and the Fox
sentences: A dog and a rooster were good friends.
One night, they slept under a big tree.
The rooster flew up to a branch.
The dog slept in a hollow at the bottom of the tree.
In the morning, the rooster crowed.
A hungry fox heard him and came to the tree.
"What a lovely song!" said the fox. "Please come down."
The rooster knew the fox was trying to trick him.
"Wake my friend at the bottom first," said the rooster. "He will show you the way up."
The fox went to find the friend.
Out jumped the dog, barking loudly.
The fox ran away as fast as he could.
Then the two friends walked on together.

credit.title: The Dog, the Cock and the Fox
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Bundle of Sticks
sentences: A farmer had three children who argued all the time.
One day, he gave them a bundle of sticks tied with a string.
"Try to break this bundle," he said.
Each child pushed and pulled, but the bundle stayed in one piece.
Then the farmer untied the string.
He gave each child one stick.
"Now try," he said.
Each stick broke with a loud snap.
"When you help each other, you are strong, like the bundle," said the farmer.
"When you argue, you are weak, like one stick."

credit.title: The Bundle of Sticks
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: Maya Reads Out Loud
sentences: Every Friday, Ms. Ortiz's class had a share time.
This week, Maya signed up to read her new comic out loud.
She was quiet in class and liked to sit at the back.
When her name was called, her face got hot.
Her hands shook as she held the paper.
For a second, she wanted to sit back down.
Then she looked at Sam, who gave her a thumbs-up.
Maya took a deep breath and began to read.
Her voice was soft at first, but it got stronger with each page.
When she read the funny part, the class laughed.
At the end, everyone clapped.
Maya sat down with a small smile.
Later, Ms. Ortiz said, "That took courage, Maya."

passages.title: The Fox and the Leopard
sentences: A fox and a leopard were resting in the shade of a tree.
The leopard looked down at his golden coat, which was covered in dark spots.
"Look at my beautiful coat," he said. "No other animal in the forest has a coat like mine."
The fox had a plain red coat, but she did not mind.
"Your coat is very handsome," she said. "But I have something that I like even more."
"What could be better than my spots?" asked the leopard.
"A quick mind," said the fox.
"Your spots are on the outside, where everyone can see them."
"My ideas are on the inside, and they help me every day."
"They help me find food, choose safe paths and solve difficult problems."
The leopard looked at his spots and said nothing for a long time.

credit.title: The Fox and the Leopard
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Oak and the Reeds
sentences: A tall oak tree grew on the bank of a wide river.
Near its roots grew a patch of thin green reeds that moved in every breeze.
"You bend every time the wind blows," the oak said proudly to the reeds.
"I am much stronger than you, and I never bend at all."
"We are not as strong as you," the reeds answered. "So we bend, and that keeps us safe."
One night, a powerful storm rushed down the valley toward the river.
The wind pushed hard against the oak, but the oak stood stiff and straight and refused to move.
The reeds bent low until their tips almost touched the water.
The wind blew harder and harder.
At last, with a loud crack, the oak fell over into the river.
In the morning, the sun came out, and the air was calm again.
One by one, the reeds stood up again, as green as before.
"I was strong," said the oak, "but I could not bend."

credit.title: The Oak and the Reeds
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: Starting Again
sentences: Since January, the Grade 6 band and the Grade 7 band had practiced one song together for the end of the spring concert.
Ana played the trumpet in the Grade 6 band, and in that last song she had a short solo, eight bars of music that she played all by herself.
Her friend Leo, the Grade 7 drummer, played the drums in that song.
At every practice together, he kept the beat steady so that both bands could follow it.
It rained on the night of the concert, so the bands played in the school gym, which was full of families.
When Ana stood up for her solo, her hands felt cold on the trumpet.
The first note came out wrong and squeaky, and several people in the audience looked up in surprise.
Ana lowered her trumpet and stared at the music on her stand.
For a moment, the only sound in the gym was Leo's drum, still keeping the beat.
Leo looked at her and nodded on each beat: one, two, three, four.
On the next count of one, Ana lifted her trumpet and began to play again.
The rest of the solo was clear and strong.
After the concert, Ana packed her trumpet into its case slowly and quietly.
"I ruined the solo," she told Leo.
"You stopped, but then you started again," Leo said. "That's the hard part."
The band teacher walked over and agreed with him.
"A band is a team," she said. "When one player stops, the others keep playing until she is ready to join again."

passages.title: The Borrowed Wheel
sentences: Priya's robotics club had built a small rover named Scout for the island's yearly robot challenge.
Each rover had to drive through a maze, pick up a block and carry it back to the starting line.
Teams from three different schools gathered in the library hall to compete.
Every team got two runs, and only the faster run counted.
On Priya's first run, Scout took a corner too quickly and crashed into the wall of the maze.
One of its plastic back wheels cracked completely in half.
Priya searched through the toolbox, but the club had forgotten to pack a spare wheel.
Her second run was scheduled to start in only ten minutes.
Then a girl from the Gull Island team walked over with a small bag of parts.
"Our rover uses the same wheels," she said. "You can have one of our spares."
Priya was surprised. "But we are trying to beat you," she said.
The girl shrugged. "It is more fun when every team gets to run."
With the borrowed wheel, Scout completed its second run, and Priya's team finished in second place.
The Gull Island team won the competition, and Priya's club applauded louder than anyone else.
On the bus ride home, Priya opened her notebook and started a careful list for the next challenge.
At the top, she wrote, "Pack extra spare parts, for us and for anyone who needs one."

passages.title: Finding the Way Without a Map
sentences: Long ago, Polynesian sailors crossed the Pacific Ocean in large canoes and found islands that were thousands of miles apart.
They had no compass, no paper maps and no machines to show them where they were.
Instead, their navigators studied the sky, the sea and the birds, and they kept everything they knew in their memories.
The stars were their most important guide.
A navigator learned the exact places where many stars rose and set along the horizon, the line where the sea meets the sky.
Each of those places marked a different direction.
During the day, navigators studied the ocean swells, which are long, steady waves that can travel across the sea for hundreds of miles.
By feeling how the canoe rocked on the swells, a navigator could tell whether the canoe was still heading the right way, even when clouds hid the sky.
Near the end of a voyage, the crew watched for clues that land was close.
Some seabirds fly out to sea to catch fish in the morning and return to land in the evening, so a canoe that followed them at sunset could find an island.
Clouds also tend to gather and stay above an island, even when the island itself is still too far away to see.
Learning all of this took many years.
Young navigators studied with older ones, first on land and then at sea, until they could picture the whole voyage in their minds.
A long voyage could last for weeks, so the crew had to trust the navigator, and the navigator had to trust years of careful practice.
Over time, fewer people learned these skills, and some of the knowledge was almost forgotten.
Then, in the 1970s, a crew built a double canoe, which is two canoes joined side by side, using an old design.
They sailed it from Hawaii to Tahiti, a trip of more than 2,000 miles, and the navigator used no compass or charts.
The voyage took about a month, and the canoe arrived safely.
Since then, many new navigators have learned the old ways, and they now teach them to younger students.

credit.title: Finding the Way Without a Map
credit.author: Learning to Fly (AI-drafted)

passages.title: The Two Halves
sentences: Every spring, heavy rain carries new stones down the creek in Story Woods.
Maya spent a whole Saturday morning searching its banks for geodes, which are round rocks that can be hollow inside and lined with crystals.
From the outside, a geode looks like a plain, bumpy gray ball, so the only way to know what is inside is to open it.
By noon, after hours of careful searching, Maya had found just one, about the size of an orange.
It felt light for its size, which is often a sign that a geode is hollow.
Near the old mill, she noticed a boy of about eight sitting on a rock beside an empty bucket.
His grandpa was sitting on a wooden bench nearby, reading a newspaper.
The boy told Maya that he had been searching since breakfast and had not found a single geode.
He said it quietly, and he kept his eyes on his empty bucket the entire time.
Maya looked down at the bumpy gray geode resting in her hand.
She had wanted a geode for her rock collection for a very long time.
But she also remembered her very first rock hunt, when she had walked home with nothing.
"Do you want to see what is inside this one?" she asked.
The boy's grandpa smiled and took out a geode cracker, a chain that wraps around a rock and squeezes it until it splits.
Maya and the boy wrapped the chain around the middle of the geode, and the grandpa slowly pressed the handles together.
With a sharp snap, the geode broke into two even halves.
Inside, both halves sparkled with small, clear quartz crystals.
Maya carefully held out one sparkling half to the boy.
"Now we both have one," she said.
The boy held his half up to the sunlight and turned it slowly, watching the crystals flash.
Maya's half was only half of a geode, but on the walk home, she felt just as happy as if she had kept the whole thing.

passages.title: The Two Goats
sentences: A narrow log lay across a deep, fast stream.
One morning, a white goat stepped onto one end of the log.
At the same moment, a black goat stepped onto the other end.
They walked carefully until they met in the middle.
"Go back," said the white goat. "I was here first."
"No, you go back," said the black goat. "I will not move for anyone."
Neither goat would go back, not even one step.
They pushed against each other with their curved horns.
The log shook, and both goats tumbled into the cold water.
They climbed out on opposite banks, dripping and shivering.
If one goat had gone back for a moment, both goats could have crossed safely.

credit.title: The Two Goats
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Boys and the Frogs
sentences: Some boys were playing beside a quiet pond.
They threw flat stones to make them skip across the water.
Each stone bounced across the surface three or four times.
The boys laughed and cheered after every throw.
But many frogs lived in the pond.
The stones splashed all around them, so the frogs hid deep in the mud.
At last, an old frog poked his head above the water.
"Please stop," he called. "This game is fun for you, but it could hurt us."
The boys looked at each other in surprise.
They had not thought about the frogs at all.
So they walked down to the river, where no frogs lived, and skipped their stones there instead.

credit.title: The Boys and the Frogs
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: Belling the Cat
sentences: A family of mice lived inside the walls of an old farmhouse.
A gray cat lived in the house too, and she loved to chase mice.
The mice worried about her all the time, so they rarely left their holes, even to look for food.
One night, the mice held a big meeting to solve their problem.
Many mice shared ideas, but none of the ideas seemed good enough.
Then a young mouse jumped up with a new suggestion.
"Let's hang a bell around the cat's neck," he said.
"Whenever she moves, the bell will ring, and we will hear her coming."
The other mice cheered and clapped for the wonderful plan.
Then an old mouse slowly stood up at the back of the room.
"It is a fine plan," she said. "But which one of us will put the bell on the cat?"
The room went completely silent.
The mice looked at each other, and then they looked down at the floor.
Not one mouse raised a paw.

credit.title: Belling the Cat
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: Two Players, One Door
sentences: On Saturday, Ben showed Maya his new video game.
It was a game for two players, and Maya had never played it before.
In the first level, the players had to jump across moving platforms.
Ben knew every jump, so he raced ahead.
Maya kept missing the platforms and starting over at the beginning.
Soon Ben reached a big door at the end of the level.
The door had two switches, one on each side.
Both switches had to be pressed at the same time.
Ben waited, but Maya was still far behind.
So he walked his player all the way back to the start.
"Watch my feet," he said, and he showed her each jump slowly.
Maya copied him, one platform at a time.
When they reached the door together, they each stood on a switch.
The door opened, and Maya laughed. "Next level!" she said.

passages.title: One Map, Many Ships
sentences: People have made detailed maps of the Moon and of Mars.
But less than a third of the floor of Earth's own ocean has been mapped in detail.
Light cannot travel far through deep water, so the bottom is too dark to photograph from above.
Instead, ships map the ocean floor with sound.
A device under the ship sends a short sound straight down.
The sound hits the bottom and bounces back to the ship.
By timing that echo, the crew can tell how deep the water is at that spot.
One ship can only map a narrow strip at a time, and the ocean is enormous.
So a worldwide project now asks every ship that can help to share its maps.
Research ships, fishing boats and even some sailboats send in what they find.
All of these strips are joined together into one big map that anyone can use for free.
Bit by bit, the empty places on the map are being filled in.

passages.title: Taking Turns at the Front
sentences: In the fall, many geese fly south together in a long V shape.
Scientists have studied why some large birds fly this way.
When a bird flaps its wings, the air just past the tips of its wings rises a little.
A bird flying just behind and to the side can ride on that rising air.
This makes flying a little easier, so the birds behind save energy.
The bird at the very front has no bird ahead of it.
So the front bird works the hardest of all.
But studies of birds flying in a V have found that they share the front place.
One bird leads for a while, and then it moves back.
Then another bird takes a turn at the front.
By sharing the hardest job, the whole flock saves energy on its long trip.

passages.title: The Long Trip to Pluto
sentences: In January 2006, a spacecraft about the size of a piano was launched toward Pluto.
Pluto is a small, icy world far out past Neptune.
The spacecraft was named New Horizons, and it had to travel about three billion miles.
The trip took more than nine years.
For much of that time, most of its machines were switched off to save power.
Every so often, the team on Earth switched them back on to check that everything still worked.
At last, in July 2015, New Horizons flew past Pluto.
It could not stop, so it took as many pictures as it could while it passed.
Because Pluto is so far away, the pictures came back to Earth very slowly.
It took more than a year for all of them to arrive.
The pictures showed tall mountains of ice and a huge pale area shaped like a heart.
No one had ever seen Pluto clearly before.

passages.title: Hercules and the Wagoner
sentences: Long ago, a farmer was driving a heavy wagon along a country road after three days of rain.
The wagon was loaded with sacks of grain for the market in town, and two strong horses pulled it.
The road had turned soft and deep with mud.
Suddenly, the front wheels sank into a muddy rut, a long groove in the road, and the wagon stopped.
The horses strained and pulled, but the wagon would not move.
The farmer climbed down and stood beside the road with his arms folded.
He did not push the wagon or even look closely at the wheels.
Instead, he looked up at the sky and called for Hercules, a hero from old Greek and Roman stories who was famous for his great strength.
"Hercules, come and help me!" he shouted. "My wagon is stuck, and I cannot move it."
After a while, Hercules appeared beside the wagon.
He looked at the farmer, and then he looked at the deep mud around the wheels.
"Put your shoulder against that wheel and push," he said. "While you push, call to your horses so that they pull at the same moment."
The farmer was surprised, but he did what Hercules said.
He pressed his shoulder against the muddy wheel and pushed as hard as he could.
At the same moment, he called to the horses, and they pulled together.
Slowly, the wheel began to turn, and then the wagon rolled up out of the rut.
When the farmer turned around to thank Hercules, the road beside him was empty.

credit.title: Hercules and the Wagoner
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Quiet Teammate
sentences: In September, a new player joined the soccer team that Ana and Ben play on.
He was tall and fast, but he hardly said a word at practice.
When other players shouted "Over here!" or "Pass it!", he stayed silent.
A few players decided that he was unfriendly, and they stopped passing the ball to him.
During a scrimmage, which is a practice game between players on the same team, Ana watched him closely.
She noticed that he did send messages, but he used his hands instead of his voice.
Right before he ran, he always pointed to the empty space where he was going.
Then he looked straight at the player who had the ball.
Nobody had been paying attention to his signals.
The next time Ana had the ball, she watched for his pointing hand.
He pointed toward the left side of the goal and started to sprint.
Ana kicked the ball into that space, and it reached him at exactly the right moment.
He scored easily.
For the rest of the scrimmage, the two of them passed the ball back and forth again and again.
After practice, the new player walked over while Ana was untying her cleats.
He gave her a thumbs-up and said two quiet words: "Good pass."
At the next practice, Ana and Ben waited for him at the field gate so that the three of them could warm up together.

passages.title: The Youngest Teacher
sentences: For three weeks, Leo had been trying to land a pop shove-it at the Harbor Town skate park.
In a pop shove-it, the rider jumps while the skateboard spins halfway around underneath, staying flat, and then the rider lands back on it.
Leo could get the board spinning, but it always spun too far or shot out to the side.
Each time he missed, he made a joke about it, but his jokes were getting shorter.
One afternoon, a girl who looked about nine years old rolled into the park.
On her very first try, she landed a perfect pop shove-it.
Leo stopped and stared.
His face felt hot, and for a moment he thought about picking up his board and going home.
He was thirteen, and she was much younger than he was.
Instead, Leo skated over to her.
"That was a great shove-it," he said. "Can you show me how you do it?"
The girl showed him how she kept her front foot light, resting near the middle of the board.
She also told him to scoop the tail backward with his back foot instead of stamping down hard.
Leo tried her way twelve times before the board finally spun halfway around and landed right under his feet.
The girl clapped, and Leo took a deep bow, like a performer at the end of a show.
Before he left, he showed her a trick that he knew well, the manual, where you roll along on just the back wheels.

passages.title: The Goatherd and the Wild Goats
sentences: One winter evening, a goatherd was leading his goats home across the hills when a heavy snowstorm began.
He hurried them into a deep cave to wait until the storm passed.
Inside the cave, he found that a small group of wild goats had already taken shelter there.
They were larger and stronger than his own goats, and the goatherd decided that he wanted to keep them.
The storm lasted for several days, and the snow piled high outside the cave.
The goatherd had brought only a little hay, so he had to choose how to share it.
He gave the wild goats almost all of it, because he hoped they would grow fond of him and stay.
His own goats, who had followed him faithfully for years, received only a few mouthfuls each.
They stood at the back of the cave and watched the wild goats eat.
At last, the snow stopped, and the sun came out over the hills.
The goatherd led the way out of the cave, expecting the wild goats to follow his flock home.
Instead, they ran straight up the mountain toward their old home.
"Wait!" he called. "I fed you better than my own goats!"
The oldest wild goat stopped on a rock and looked back at him.
"That is exactly why we are leaving," she said. "Your own goats followed you for years, and you gave them almost nothing as soon as we arrived."
"If new goats come along next winter, you will treat us the same way."

credit.title: The Goatherd and the Wild Goats
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Cleaning Station
sentences: On a coral reef, some small fish have an unusual job: they clean other fish.
One of the best known is the cleaner wrasse, a slim fish with a dark stripe along its side.
Each cleaner wrasse stays at one spot on the reef, which scientists call a cleaning station.
Bigger fish swim to the station and wait their turn, a bit like customers waiting at a shop.
When it is a fish's turn, it holds still and often opens its mouth and gills wide.
The cleaner swims all over the fish's body, even inside its mouth, and eats tiny pests called parasites.
The big fish gets cleaned, and the small fish gets a meal.
Some visitors, such as groupers, usually eat small fish, but at the cleaning station they leave the cleaner alone.
Scientists who watch cleaning stations have noticed something else.
Sometimes a cleaner cheats.
It bites off a bit of the healthy slime that coats the visitor's skin, because it likes that taste better.
When that happens, the visitor jerks away and may swim off.
Studies suggest that fish waiting nearby notice this, and they are more likely to visit cleaners that do not cheat.
Cleaners also seem to do a more careful job when other fish are watching.

passages.title: The Jackdaw and the Borrowed Feathers
sentences: A jackdaw is a small black bird with pale gray eyes, a cousin of the crow.
One jackdaw often flew over the garden of a large palace, where the king kept a flock of peacocks.
He admired their long, shining tail feathers, which were blue and green and covered with bright spots shaped like eyes.
Compared to them, his own plain black feathers seemed dull, and he began to feel ashamed of them.
Once a year, peacocks shed their long tail feathers, and many of them lay scattered across the palace lawn.
The jackdaw collected as many as he could carry and carefully tucked them in among his own feathers.
Then he strutted into the garden and walked among the peacocks as if he were one of them.
When his old jackdaw friends called to him from the palace wall, he turned his head away and pretended not to hear.
At first, the peacocks were puzzled by the strange little bird.
Then one of them recognized a feather with a bent tip that she had lost only the week before.
The peacocks gathered around the jackdaw and pulled their feathers back out, one by one.
Soon he stood on the lawn as he really was, a small black bird.
The jackdaw flew back to the palace wall to join his old friends.
But they remembered how he had turned away from them, and they did not make room for him on the wall.
He sat alone at the far end, plain and black, wishing he had never borrowed a single feather.

credit.title: The Vain Jackdaw and his Borrowed Feathers
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: Biscuit's Window
sentences: For eighteen years, an orange cat named Biscuit lived at the Lighthouse Café.
Every morning, he slept in a patch of sunlight on the front window seat, and customers stopped to stroke his soft fur.
Mrs. Lin, who owns the café, gave him a small breakfast each day before she unlocked the door.
Biscuit was very old, and in March he died quietly in his sleep.
The next Saturday, Maya and Sam went to the café for hot chocolate, as they often did.
The window seat was empty, and Mrs. Lin was quieter than usual.
Sam wanted to say something kind, but every sentence he thought of sounded wrong in his head.
Maya did not know what to say either, so the two friends drank their hot chocolate in silence.
At home that night, Maya took out her sketchbook.
She drew Biscuit curled up asleep in his patch of sunlight, with the harbor behind him.
She took her time with the colors, so that his fur was the same warm orange she remembered.
On Monday after school, she gave the drawing to Mrs. Lin without saying a word.
Mrs. Lin looked at it for a long time.
Then she held Maya's hand for a moment and said softly, "That is exactly how he looked."
The next week, the drawing hung in a small frame beside the cash register, where every customer could see it.

passages.title: Test Number Twenty-Three
sentences: For its spring showcase, the robotics club set a challenge: each member had to build a robot arm that could pick up a raw egg and set it gently in an egg carton.
The arm had to lift the egg from a bowl, swing it across the table and let go without a single crack.
Priya built an arm with a small motor at each joint and a two-fingered gripper at the end.
She named it Feather, because she wanted its touch to be that light.
On the first test, the gripper squeezed so hard that the egg cracked before it even left the bowl.
Priya did not start rebuilding right away.
Instead, she wiped up the egg, opened a notebook and wrote down exactly what had happened: the grip was too strong.
For the second test, she changed only one thing, setting the gripper motor to close more gently.
This time Feather lifted the egg, but halfway across the table the egg slipped out and rolled away.
Test after test, Priya followed the same pattern: try, watch carefully, write it down and change one thing.
She glued soft foam pads to the gripper's fingers, slowed down the swing of the arm and added a sensor that stopped the fingers when they touched the shell.
Some changes helped, and others made things worse, so she undid those and recorded them too.
By the end of the second week, her notebook described twenty-two tests, and not one egg had reached the carton in one piece.
On the morning of the showcase, Priya read through every page of her notes.
She noticed that every egg that slipped had fallen at the same moment, just as the arm started to swing.
So she changed the program to make the arm start its swing very slowly and then speed up.
On test twenty-three, Feather lifted the egg, carried it smoothly across the table and set it in the carton without a crack.
The club cheered, and Leo, who had come to watch, asked whether Feather could flip pancakes next.
Priya laughed and turned to a fresh page in her notebook.

passages.title: The Rain Gauge Volunteers
sentences: Every morning at about the same time, thousands of volunteers around the world step outside to check a simple tool in their yards.
The tool is a rain gauge, a tall, clear tube that catches rain and shows how much has fallen.
Some volunteers also read a thermometer that records the highest and lowest temperatures of the day.
They write the numbers down or send them to a weather service, even on days when the gauge is completely empty.
One reading by itself does not tell scientists very much.
A single backyard might get a heavy shower while a neighborhood three miles away stays completely dry.
But when thousands of readings are put together, they form a detailed picture of where rain fell and how much.
Forecasters use these reports to plan for floods and dry spells, and farmers use them to decide when to water their crops.
Some volunteers have kept their records for more than fifty years, through snowstorms, heat waves and pouring rain.
Their long lists of numbers allow scientists to compare today's weather with the weather of many years ago.
In some places, the records go back more than a hundred years, because one volunteer handed the job on to the next.
Most of these volunteers are not famous, and few people ever see their notebooks.
Many of them say the job takes only a few minutes a day.
Yet without all those quiet minutes, added up over many years, forecasters and scientists would know far less about the weather.

passages.title: The Salt Hall
sentences: Near the city of Kraków in Poland, there is a salt mine where people dug rock salt for about seven hundred years.
Long ago, salt was so valuable that people sometimes called it white gold, because they needed it to keep meat and fish from spoiling.
Over the centuries, miners dug more than one hundred miles of tunnels and large rooms deep under the ground.
The miners did more than dig.
Using simple hand tools, some of them began to carve the salt walls around them into statues and pictures.
The most famous carving is a huge underground hall, more than three hundred feet below the surface.
Almost everything in it is made of salt: the floor, the stairs, the carved pictures on the walls and many statues.
Even the large chandeliers that hang from the ceiling are made of salt crystals.
Miners worked on this hall for more than thirty years, carving it a little at a time.
Rock salt is softer than most stone, but it is still slow work to carve.
One wrong cut can crack a figure that has taken months to shape, so the carvers had to be patient and careful.
The work was passed from one carver to the next, and each one continued what the last had started.
Mining for salt there ended about thirty years ago, but the tunnels did not close.
Today, visitors walk down hundreds of steps to see the salt hall, and some say it is the most beautiful room they have ever seen.
Every carving they see was made one small cut at a time.

passages.title: One Hundred Players, One Song
sentences: Trinidad and Tobago is a small island country in the Caribbean Sea, and its national instrument is the steelpan.
A steelpan is made from a large metal oil drum.
Pan makers hammer the top of the drum into a deep bowl and then shape small areas on it, and each area plays a different note.
People on the islands began making these instruments in the 1930s and 1940s, using metal cans and drums that had been thrown away.
Steelpans come in many sizes.
Small, high pans play the melody, while the deepest bass pans are so large that one player may stand surrounded by six whole drums.
A big steel band, which is also called a steel orchestra, can have more than one hundred players.
Each player has only a small part of the music, and on its own, a single part may not sound much like a song.
Every year, before the islands' Carnival festival, steel bands enter a large music contest.
For weeks beforehand, the players gather almost every night in outdoor practice spaces called panyards.
Many of them learn their parts by listening and copying, while a leader teaches one section of the band at a time.
Some players are teenagers, some are grandparents, and many have played with the same band for years.
Slowly, over many nights, the separate parts begin to fit together.
On the night of the contest, the band rolls its pans onto the stage on racks with wheels.
When the music starts, the high pans, the middle pans and the bass pans join into one huge sound that people can feel as well as hear.
The crowd hears one song, but it is really more than a hundred small parts played together.

passages.title: The New Order Screen
sentences: In September, Grandma Rose bought a tablet for the counter at Rose's Bakery, so that she could type in cake orders instead of writing them on paper slips.
Sam came over after school to help her learn it, because he was quick with screens.
The first afternoon did not go well.
Every time Grandma Rose paused to read a button, Sam reached over and tapped it for her.
When she typed a customer's name too slowly, he took the tablet and finished it himself.
By the end of the afternoon, five orders were saved perfectly, but Grandma Rose could not remember how to make a single one.
She pressed her lips together and said that she would go back to paper slips.
That night, Sam thought about the afternoon.
He realized that Grandma Rose had not learned anything, because he had done every step for her.
The next day, he brought five index cards to the bakery.
On each card, he wrote one step in large letters and drew a picture of the button to press.
Then he sat on a stool beside her and kept his hands in his lap.
Grandma Rose went slowly, and twice she pressed the wrong button and had to go back.
Each time, Sam waited and pointed to the card instead of the screen.
On Saturday morning, the bakery was crowded, and a man wanted a chocolate cake that said "Happy Birthday, Grandpa."
Grandma Rose typed the whole order herself, without looking at a single card.
When the man left, she looked across the room at Sam, who was filling bags with cinnamon rolls, and gave him a thumbs-up.

passages.title: The Fossil That Was Glued Together
sentences: In 1999, a fossil went on display that seemed to answer a big question about dinosaurs and birds.
The flat slab of rock showed the skeleton of a small animal with the wings and chest of a bird and the long, bony tail of a dinosaur.
A famous magazine said it showed how dinosaurs and birds were joined, and pictures of it spread around the world.
But the fossil had been bought from a dealer, and no one had checked it carefully before it was announced.
When scientists finally studied the slab closely, some things did not fit.
A scanner that uses X-rays to see inside solid things showed that the slab was made of many separate pieces.
Someone had glued them together and filled the cracks with paste, probably so that it would look whole and sell for more money.
Then a scientist found another fossil whose tail matched the tail on the slab exactly, and it belonged to a completely different animal.
The magazine had to tell its readers that it had been wrong.
It was an awkward moment, but scientists learned a lesson from it.
Today, many scientists will not study a fossil until they know exactly where it came from and are sure that it has not been changed.
The story also had a surprise ending.
Once the pieces were taken apart and studied honestly, the tail turned out to belong to a small feathered dinosaur that no one had ever named before.
The front half was a real early bird.
The truth gave scientists two real animals to study instead of one that never existed.
